title: Epistolae
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0162.stoa004.opp-lat4, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Visa hæc est olim Erasmo non ebhorrere a stylo Tertulliani, quantum, inquit, ex illius fragmentis licet odovari ; eat enim affectatior et duriusculus , etiumbi gravibus sententiis. Existimantalii, fortasse r'tiamcongruenter magis, ad subsequentis dictionem Epistolæ , quæ, nemine jam diffitente , S.
passages.english: It once seemed to Erasmus that this [letter] is not far removed from the style of Tertullian, as far, he says, as one may judge by scent from his fragments; for it is rather affected and somewhat harsh, though with weighty sentences. Others think, perhaps even more fittingly, that it comes so close to the diction of the following Letter, which, as no one now denies, is St.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ebhorrere' for 'abhorrere', 'odovari' for 'odorari', 'eat' for 'est', 'etiumbi' for 'etiamsi', 'r'tiamcongruenter' for 'etiam congruenter'. The sentence continues into the following context ('...Maximi Taurinensis est', i.e. [the work] of Maximus of Turin).

passages.original: Quem talis cogitatio non cum admiratione delectet? Reliquias, inquam, corporum nostrorum, aut nullas aut minimas certe, et quantulascumque : attamen sordidas, et animi numquam sine horrore inspectas, in suum iterum hominem, non ut Pythagoras mentiens et delirans in Euphorbo essecredatur, sed in proprium suum corpus et nomen, per ossa, et nervos, per venas, per cuncta vitalia, non modo artuatim, verum etiam articulatim recompaginandum.
passages.english: Whom would such a thought not delight, together with wonder? The remains, I say, of our bodies, either none at all or certainly very small, and however slight; and yet filthy, and never looked upon by the mind without horror, [are] to be joined together again into their own man, not, as Pythagoras, lying and raving, is believed to have been in Euphorbus, but into its own proper body and name, through bones and sinews, through veins, through all the vital parts, not only limb by limb but also joint by joint.
passages.notes: 'essecredatur' read as 'esse credatur'. The sentence lacks a main verb; the gerundive 'recompaginandum' implies 'are to be reassembled'.

passages.original: nescientes quod in sanctis Dei, nartyribus, confessoribusque oculi ejus pupilla feriatur? Peribunt sine dubio, peribunt in illa die omnes cogitationes eorum : nec eos apud tribunal illud aut Lucius Crassus defendet, aut M. Antonius, aut istis eloquentior Tullius : quoniam omnis tunc saeculi lingua obmutescet, et sola erit in rusticulis suis facunda justilia : quae infantium fecit ora diserta, et mutorum linguas novum solvit in canticum, coelestemque sibi harmoniam per sui misericordiam de suis oviculis acquisivit.
passages.english: not knowing that in the saints of God, the martyrs and confessors, the pupil of his eye is struck? They will perish without doubt, all their thoughts will perish on that day; and before that tribunal neither Lucius Crassus nor Marcus Antonius will defend them, nor Tully, more eloquent than these; for then every tongue of the world will fall silent, and justice alone will be eloquent in its rustic little ones: [justice] which made the mouths of infants articulate, and loosed the tongues of the mute into a new song, and through its mercy acquired for itself a heavenly harmony from its own little sheep.
passages.notes: 'nartyribus' read as 'martyribus', 'justilia' as 'justitia'. The passage begins mid-sentence.

passages.original: Et quia et ipsi daemones operantur, intelligere naturas, quae vera sint, quæ falsa, qaae novisse, est non decipi, non errare, non inimico assignare quae Dei Bunt, nee Deo adjudicare, quæ sunt dæmonum : scire tempora, signa cognosiere, habere Domini cognitam voluntatem : et alia Dei mirabilia cum gratiarum actione venerari, alia cum digna execratione vitare. Talem virum eliam sæculi homines laudavere, dicente Virgilio :
passages.english: And since the demons themselves also work [wonders], [it is fine] to understand the natures [of things], which are true, which false; to know which is not to be deceived, not to err, not to assign to the enemy the things that are God's, nor to award to God the things that are the demons'; to know the times, to recognise the signs, to have the Lord's will known; and to venerate some of God's wonders with thanksgiving, to shun others with fitting execration. Even men of the world have praised such a man, as Virgil says:
passages.notes: Construction depends on the preceding 'quam pulchrum est' (how fine it is); syntax is loose. 'qaae' read 'quae', 'Bunt' 'sunt', 'cognosiere' 'cognoscere'. The Virgil quotation is not included in the text.

passages.original: (Habetur etiam apud Augustinum in Appendice tomi VI, inscripta Sermo in Psalmum XLI, ad Neophytos. Erasm us ait: Apparet hoc fragmentum esse ex Hom iliis alicujus in psalmos mysticos ergo loc. cit.): certe nihil babet Hieronymianum. , Videsis
passages.english: (It is also found in Augustine, in the Appendix to volume VI, entitled Sermon on Psalm 41, to the Neophytes. Erasmus says: It appears that this fragment is from the Homilies of someone on the mystical psalms, therefore loc. cit.): certainly it has nothing of Jerome about it. See
passages.notes: Editorial note; 'mysticos ergo loc. cit.' appears garbled and its sense is uncertain. 'Videsis' (see) is left incomplete.

passages.original: Bombulum itaque cum fistulis, id est, doctor in medio Ecclesiæ est, cum Spiritu sancto, qai loquitur in eo : constringitur in ligno alto, id est, Christo, qui a sapientibus ligno vitæ comparatur : in catena, id est, in fide : et non tangit terram, id est, opera carnalia : duodecim bombula, id est, duode. cim apostoli : cum fistulis, id est, divinis eloquiis. Cithara de qua in quadragesimo secundo psalmo scriptum est : Confitebor libi in cithara, Deus, Deus meus (Psal. XLII, 4), propriæ consuetudinis est apud Hebræos, quae cum chordis viginti quatuor, quæ in modum Deltæ litterae, sicut peritissimi tradunt, utique componitur : et per digitos Pindari variis vocibus tinnulis ictibusque in diversis nodis concitatur.
passages.english: The bombulum with pipes, then, is the teacher in the midst of the Church, with the Holy Spirit who speaks in him; it is bound to a high wooden pole, that is, to Christ, who by the wise is compared to the tree of life; by a chain, that is, by faith; and it does not touch the earth, that is, carnal works; the twelve bombula, that is, the twelve apostles; with pipes, that is, with the divine words. The cithara, of which it is written in the forty-second psalm: I will confess to you on the cithara, O God, my God (Ps. 42:4), is of a type peculiar to the Hebrews; it is constructed with twenty-four strings, in the shape of the letter Delta, as the most expert report, and it is set sounding by the fingers of the player with various ringing notes and strokes on different knots.
passages.notes: *bombulum*: an unidentified sounding instrument (bells/pipes). 'per digitos Pindari' literally 'by the fingers of Pindar'; likely corrupt or meaning a musician generally; sense uncertain.

passages.original: III. Ego autem in Domino sperans adjicio, quod Ulyssis imitator eris, non Empedoclis : qui, per suam philosophiam (ne dicam melancholiam, id est, atram bilem) victus, Ætuam sibi mausoleum elegit: et parabolam quam audis, ad veteres attulit : ideo taccre non possum. Tandem validior est ille ignis tuus, quod tibi annuit pars adversa : quam vereor aestus ille tuus, quo in me accenderis, ne minorem major ad se trahat : Et propterea loqui prohibeor.
passages.english: III. But I, hoping in the Lord, add that you will be an imitator of Ulysses, not of Empedocles, who, overcome by his philosophy (not to say his melancholy, that is, black bile), chose Etna as his tomb; and he brought to the ancients the parable which you hear: therefore I cannot keep silent. At length that fire of yours is stronger, because the opposing party nods assent to you; but I fear that heat of yours, with which you are inflamed against me, lest the greater draw the lesser to itself: and for this reason I am forbidden to speak.
passages.notes: This passage is from a spurious letter and its sense is obscure; the logic of 'ideo tacere non possum' followed by 'loqui prohibeor' seems contradictory, and the text may be corrupt. 'Ætuam' is read as 'Aetnam' and 'taccre' as 'tacere'; 'quam vereor' is construed loosely as 'but I fear'.

passages.original: XVI. Cicero post repudium Terentiae uxorari noluit, dicens se pariter uxori et philosophiae operam dare non posse. Amice, utinam tibi hoc animus tuus respondeat, vel tua lingua mihi: ut loquendo saltem eloquentiæ principem digneris imitari, et mihi spem facias ,vel vanam.
passages.english: XVI. Cicero, after divorcing Terentia, refused to marry, saying that he could not devote himself equally to a wife and to philosophy. Friend, would that your mind would give you this answer, or your tongue give it to me: so that at least in speech you might deign to imitate the prince of eloquence, and give me hope, even if vain.
passages.notes: 'uxorari' read as 'uxorem ducere'/'uxorari' (to take a wife).

passages.original: XVIII. Pacuvius nens, ait Arrio vicino suo, Amice, arborem habeo in horto mco infelicem, de qua prima uxor mea se suspendit : postmodum sccunda, jam nunc tertia. Cui Arriuc: Miror te in tot successibus lacrymas iuvcnisse. Et iterum : Dii boni, quot tibi, dispendia arbor illa sucpendit.
passages.english: XVIII. Pacuvius, weeping, said to his neighbour Arrius: "Friend, I have in my garden an unlucky tree, from which my first wife hanged herself, afterwards my second, and now just now my third." Arrius [replied] to him: "I am surprised that amid so many successes you have found [cause for] tears." And again: "Good gods, how many losses that tree has hung up for you!"
passages.notes: 'nens' is read as 'flens' (weeping). 'iuvcnisse' is read as 'invenisse'. 'dispendia ... suspendit' is a pun: the tree has 'hung up' (that is, suspended or cancelled) expenses for him.

passages.original: XX. Ait Cato Uticensis : Si absque femina posset es: e mundus, conversatio nostra non esset absque diis. Amice, Cato non ubi vera et cognita loquebatur, nec quisquam feminarum exsecratur ludibria, nisi lusus et expertus, et conscius poenæ.
passages.english: XX. Cato of Utica says: If the world could exist without woman, our way of life would not be without the gods. Friend, Cato [spoke] only where he spoke things true and known, and no one curses the mockeries of women unless he has been mocked, has experienced them, and is aware of the punishment.
passages.notes: 'non ubi' probably corrupt (perhaps 'nonnisi'); rendered as 'only where'. 'es: e' read as 'esse'.

passages.original: llieronymus. Super animæ statu memini vestræ quæstiunculæ, immo maximæ ecclesiasticae quaestionis. Utrum lapsa de caelo sit, ut Pythagoras philosophus, omnesque Platonici, et Origenes putant : an a propria Dei substantia, ut Stoici, Manichaeus , et insana Priscilliani hæresis suspicantur : an in thesauro Dei habeantur olim conditæ, ut quidam Ecclesiastici stulta persuasione confidunt : an quotidie a Deo fiant , et mittantur in corpora , secundum illud quod in Evangelio scriptum est: Paler meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor : an certe ex traduce, ut Terulllianus, A pollinarius. et maxima pars Oeci- dentalium autumant, ut quomodo corpus ex corpore, sic anima nascatur ex anima : et simili cum brutii animantibus conditione subsistat.
passages.english: Jerome. On the state of the soul, I remember your little question, or rather the greatest question of the Church: whether it fell from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, and all the Platonists, and Origen think; or [comes] from God's own substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus, and the insane heresy of Priscillian suppose; or whether [souls] are kept in God's treasury, created long ago, as certain churchmen confidently believe out of foolish persuasion; or whether they are made by God daily and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel: My Father works until now, and I work; or certainly by transmission, as Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greatest part of the Westerners claim, so that as body [is born] from body, so soul is born from soul, and it subsists in a condition like that of the brute animals.

passages.original: llieronYnlus. Antonius, oratur egregius, in cujus laudibus Tullius personat, disertos se ait vidisse multos, eloquentem adhuc neminem. Noli igitur mihi oratorum, et non tuis floribus fudere, per quos solent imperitorum atque puerorum aures decipi : sed simpliciter dic quid sentias.
passages.english: Jerome. Antonius, the outstanding orator, in whose praises Tully resounds, says he had seen many fluent men, but no one yet eloquent. Do not, then, pour out on me the flowers of orators, and not your own, by which the ears of the unlearned and of boys are usually deceived; but say simply what you think.

passages.original: Augustinus.. Qui animas ex una propagari asserunt, quam Deus homini primo dedit, atque ita eas ex ps- rentibus trahi dicunt, si Tertulliani opinionem sequuntur, profecto eas non spiritus, sed corpora esse contendunt, et corpulentis seminibus exoriri : quo perversiu. quid potest dici?
passages.english: Augustine: Those who assert that souls are propagated from the one [soul] which God gave to the first man, and so say that they are drawn from the parents, if they follow the opinion of Tertullian, certainly contend that they are not spirits but bodies, and arise from bodily seeds. What can be said that is more perverse than this?
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ps- rentibus' read as 'parentibus', 'perversiu.' as 'perversius'.

passages.original: Testes autem idonei quos ad hanc rem corroborandam concitavit hi sunt Gregorius Nazianzenus mirabilis doctor, Cyrillus, Athanasius, Tbeophi!us, Anatolius, Joannes Chrysostomus, Eustathius [Al. Euslachius], Eusebius chronographus, et noster Hilarius : qui omnes uno ore eademque consensu veluti vera sancti Spiritus organa, anathematis mu- crone censent esse feriendos, qui in usu laicorum panes oblationum contulerint : quia omnino sacerdotibus solis debentur : nisi forte religionis gratia, laici pro benedictione de manu sacerdotis accipian.
passages.english: Now the suitable witnesses whom he has summoned to confirm this matter are these: Gregory of Nazianzus, the admirable teacher, Cyril, Athanasius, Theophilus, Anatolius, John Chrysostom, Eustathius [another reading: Eustachius], Eusebius the chronographer, and our own Hilary. All of these, with one mouth and the same agreement, as true instruments of the Holy Spirit, judge that those who have handed over the loaves of the offerings for the use of lay people are to be struck with the sword of anathema, because they are owed entirely to the priests alone; unless perhaps, for the sake of religion, lay people receive [them] as a blessing from the hand of the priest.
passages.notes: 'concitavit' (he has summoned): the subject is unclear from the passage alone. 'accipian.' read as 'accipiant'.

passages.original: ab iis quasdam, quas vel ex aliorum doctorum scriptis, vel ex styli, sententiarumque distantia, titulo tanti viri comperi- mus indignas : ex quibus ilia est, cujus est titulus ad DEMETRIADEM, hoc habens initium : Si summo ill- genio , parique fretus scientia. Hanc quippe B. Au- gustinns in opere contra Pelagium de Gratia Christi et de Peccato originali, ejusdem Pelagii esse dicit, quædam ipsius c frusta tractatu suo interserens, atque redarguens. Huic adduntur et istae, ad TITIA- NUM de morte filiæ, cujus initium tale est : Charitatis tuæ scripta percepi. Ad OcEANUM consolotaria, tale habens initium : Diversorum opprobria, tribulationes multiplices.
passages.english: [We have cut away] from these certain [letters] which, either from the writings of other teachers or from the difference of style and of thought, we found unworthy of the name of so great a man. Among them is the one whose title is To Demetrias, having this beginning: "If, relying on the highest talent and equal knowledge." For the blessed Augustine, in his work against Pelagius, On the Grace of Christ and On Original Sin, says that this [letter] belongs to the same Pelagius, inserting certain fragments of it into his treatise and refuting them. To this are added also these: To Titianus on the death of his daughter, whose beginning is as follows: "I have received the writings of your charity." To Oceanus, a consolatory [letter], having this beginning: "The reproaches of various [people], manifold tribulations."
passages.notes: The sentence begins in the preceding context ('Abscidimus autem'), and '[We have cut away]' supplies that verb. 'ill- genio' is read as 'ingenio'. The stray 'c' before 'frusta' is taken as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: Ad CELANTIAM, sic incipiens, Veteris scripturæ celebrata sententia eat. Hæc stylo quidem nobi- Hore est scripta; sed nec sic B. Hieronymo digna. Postrema est, Dt origine animæ dispulatio, quasi ill- ter B. Hieronymum et Augustinum : uhi licet multa ex eorum scriptis ponantur, falsa tamen est : tum quia praefati doctores numquam inter se praesentia- liter sunt locuti : tum quia eadem quæstio nec apud eos, nec apud cæteros fidei cathołicæ sectatores ad.
passages.english: To CELANTIA, beginning thus: 'It is a celebrated saying of the old Scripture.' This is indeed written in a nobler style, but even so it is not worthy of blessed Jerome. The last is 'A Disputation on the Origin of the Soul', as if between blessed Jerome and Augustine. Although many things from their writings are set in it, it is nevertheless false: both because the aforesaid teachers never spoke with each other face to face, and because this same question could not, either among them or among the other followers of the catholic faith, [be clearly defined] up to...
passages.notes: The final sentence continues in the following passage ('hac usque potuit liquido definiri', '...this time be clearly defined'). The bracketed completion is supplied from that context. Scanning errors corrected: 'eat' read as 'est', 'nobi- Hore' as 'nobiliore', 'Dt' as 'De', 'dispulatio' as 'disputatio', 'ill- ter' as 'inter', 'uhi' as 'ubi'.
